name: The Theory of Island Biogeography
statement: An island's species count settles where new arrivals balance local extinctions.
meaning: The equilibrium theory of island biogeography holds that the number of species on an island reflects a dynamic balance between the rate at which new species immigrate and the rate at which species already present go extinct. At equilibrium the two rates match, so the total number of species stays roughly constant even as the particular species present continually turn over. Larger islands and islands closer to the mainland hold more species.
mechanism: MacArthur rendered the idea as two crossing curves plotted against the number of species present. The immigration rate falls as more species are already there, since fewer remain in the mainland pool to be new arrivals; the extinction rate rises as more species crowd in, through competition and smaller populations. The two curves cross at an equilibrium number. Area shifts the extinction curve — larger islands, with bigger populations, lose species more slowly — while distance shifts the immigration curve — nearer islands are easier to reach — so both larger and closer islands settle at more species.

examples.text: Simberloff and Wilson fumigated small mangrove islets in the Florida Keys to remove their arthropods, then watched them recolonise within about a year to roughly their former species numbers but with different species — support for both equilibrium and turnover.

After the 1883 eruption sterilised the Krakatau islands, naturalists tracked the return of plants and animals, a natural test of the equilibrium model, though whether the birds reached a true equilibrium is debated.
The empirical species-area relationship, that species number rises as a power of area, pairs with the theory, though it is older and logically independent of it.

variants.name: The SLOSS debate
variants.text: The application to reserve design, asking whether a single large or several small reserves protect more species, drawn from the area-and-extinction logic but never resolved and now seen as context-dependent.

variants.name: The general dynamic model
variants.text: A later extension for oceanic islands that adds the birth, growth, and erosion of islands over geological time and the role of in-situ speciation, which the original theory ignores.

whyItMatters: It reshaped biogeography from a static, descriptive discipline into a dynamic, predictive one, giving simple rules for how area and isolation govern diversity. Its reach extends far beyond islands to habitat fragments and reserve design in conservation biology, and its crossing-curves model remains a touchstone for thinking about immigration, extinction, and the balance between them.

working.text: expect more species on larger and less isolated islands, and use area and distance to anticipate a system's equilibrium diversity.
look for the identity of species to keep changing even where their number holds steady, the theory's distinctive prediction.
treat habitat patches as islands only loosely, since the surrounding matrix and edge effects make them differ from true islands.

limits: Wilson himself judged the theory oversimplified and incomplete. Its equilibrium assumption and the reality of turnover have been questioned, and real islands' species numbers are driven by habitat diversity, not area alone, since larger islands tend to hold more habitats. The theory treats species as interchangeable, assumes immigration and extinction are independent, and ignores speciation on large or remote islands, where adaptive radiations matter. Its application to reserve design was heavily criticised, and the SLOSS debate over whether single large or several small reserves are better was never resolved.
misreadings: Equilibrium does not mean the same species persist — only the number is stable, while composition turns over. The theory does not prove a single large reserve is always best; that inference is contested and unresolved. The species-area relationship is not part of the MacArthur-Wilson theory but an older, independent empirical pattern. And the area and distance effects were observed before them; their contribution was the dynamic, equilibrium explanation.
origin: Set out by Robert MacArthur and Edward O. Wilson in a 1963 paper in Evolution and their 1967 book 'The Theory of Island Biogeography'; tested by Simberloff and Wilson's mangrove defaunation experiments in the Florida Keys.
namedAfter: Robert MacArthur and Edward O. Wilson

sources.text: The Theory of Island Biogeography, Wikipedia. — the immigration-extinction equilibrium, the area and distance effects, turnover, and the SLOSS application.
MacArthur & Wilson, "An Equilibrium Theory of Insular Zoogeography," Evolution 17(4):373-387 (1963). — the founding statement of the theory.
Simberloff & Wilson, "Experimental Zoogeography of Islands: Defaunation and Monitoring Techniques," Ecology (1969). — the mangrove defaunation test of equilibrium and turnover.
